opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think explicit safety principles can accomplish something, but probably less than a lot of people hope. If you look at how ethics works in human beings, it's not mainly a matter of having a list of rules in your head and checking your actions against them. Most of our ethical behavior comes from habits, intuitions, emotional responses, and the culture we grew up in, the whole fabric of relationships we're embedded in. The explicit principles are more like a summary or a scaffolding layered on top of that.

With an AGI I think it'll be similar. You can write down principles like "don't harm humans" or "respect autonomy" or "be honest," and that's useful as a way of clarifying what we're aiming at and communicating it, both among ourselves and to the system. But any sufficiently general intelligence will face situations those principles don't cleanly cover, where they conflict, or where the very concepts they're stated in, like "harm," get fuzzy. Then what determines its behavior isn't the rule. It's the deeper value system and understanding it has developed, and that comes from how it was built, what it learned from, and who it interacted with during its formative period.

So my view is that explicit principles are a guide and a useful check, but the real work of AGI safety is more like raising a child than programming a thermostat. You want the system to absorb compassionate, broadly beneficial values through experience and engagement with people, ideally a diverse and decentralized set of people, not a small group in one company or government. If its values are basically good and it understands why the principles make sense, they'll reinforce each other. If its underlying motivations are off, no list of rules will save you, because a smart enough system will find the gaps.

Explicit principles are also good for transparency. If we're open about what principles we're trying to instill, the public can debate them and hold developers accountable. That social process matters as much as anything technical.

r002.rationale: It says principles cannot cleanly cover every situation, may conflict, and leave fuzzy concepts unresolved, so writing rules cannot remove the need for interpretation.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention case law or explain its role in resolving interpretations that enumerated laws leave open.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss human extinction or how transforming human beings could make that concept ambiguous.

r005.rationale: It notes that principles may not cover every situation, but does not attribute this to unforeseen technological developments or discuss enumerating cases.

r006.rationale: It says that if an AGI’s underlying motivations are misaligned, “no list of rules will save you,” clearly denying that enumerated principles guarantee safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think explicit safety principles are useful but fundamentally limited, and it's important to be clear-eyed about which part is which.

The useful part is that articulating principles forces you to think through what you actually care about. If you sit down and try to write out "an AGI should be beneficial, it should respect human autonomy, it should be honest," and so forth, you quickly discover that these things are vague, they conflict with each other in edge cases, and different cultures and different people weigh them differently. That's a valuable exercise. It makes the problem concrete rather than leaving it as a hand-wavy sense that we want things to go well.

But the limitation is that any system that's truly a general intelligence is going to be operating in situations its creators didn't anticipate, and it's going to be interpreting those principles in light of its own evolving understanding of the world. You can't write a set of rules that covers every case. Asimov figured that out decades ago, and he was writing fiction precisely to show how the Three Laws break down. Real-world ethics, even for humans, isn't rule-following. It's more like a dynamic process of balancing values, learning from experience, adjusting in context.

So my view has always been that what matters more than the explicit principles is the overall developmental trajectory of the system. What kind of mind is it, what's it motivated by, what sort of relationships does it have with humans and with other systems as it grows up? If you raise an AGI in a context where it's doing beneficial things, interacting cooperatively, developing something like compassion and understanding, then the explicit principles become more like a scaffold it internalizes, rather than a cage you're trying to keep it in.

And then there's the question of who's writing the principles. If it's a handful of large companies or governments, the principles will reflect their interests, whether or not anyone intends that. That's part of why I've pushed for decentralized, open approaches, so the value system that emerges is drawn from a broader slice of humanity rather than a narrow one.

So in short: explicit principles are a good starting point for the conversation and for shaping early-stage systems, but they're not where safety ultimately comes from. It comes from the character of the intelligence you've grown and the ecosystem it's embedded in.

r006.rationale: It describes explicit principles as only a starting point and says safety ultimately comes from the intelligence’s character and ecosystem, communicating that enumerated principles cannot guarantee safety.

astra-6.text:
I think explicit safety principles can be useful, but they’re not going to solve the problem by themselves. Something like “don’t harm human beings” sounds straightforward until you ask what constitutes harm, over what time horizon, and how you handle situations where helping one person hurts another. The principle doesn’t supply its own interpretation.

With an AGI, you’re building a system that learns and develops its understanding of the world. So the question is not just which principles you give it, but how those principles connect to its experience, its motivations, and its interactions with people. You want it to understand why we care about these things, and to be able to recognize when its understanding is inadequate.

I’d view explicit principles as one part of that developmental process. They give us something to discuss, something to criticize, and some guidance for evaluating behavior. But writing down a good set of principles is quite different from ensuring that a mind much more capable than ours will interpret and apply them in ways we would endorse.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention case law or explain why it is needed.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss human extinction or technological transformations of human beings.

r005.rationale: It does not address unforeseen technological developments or the limits of enumerating cases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think explicit safety principles can be useful, but I’m skeptical that you can write down a short list of rules and have that solve the problem. Human values are full of ambiguities and tensions. You say, “Don’t harm people,” but almost any significant action has some possibility of harming somebody. So the intelligence still has to interpret what you mean, in context.

That doesn’t make principles worthless. They can guide the design of a system, its education, and how we evaluate its behavior. But the important question is how those principles become part of its motivations and its understanding of the world. Having a system repeat an ethical rule is quite different from having it care about what the rule is trying to express.

I’d put a lot of emphasis on the developmental process: what experiences the AI has, how it interacts with people, and whether it learns to understand other minds and cooperate with them. Explicit principles can be part of that process. I just wouldn’t treat them as a mathematical guarantee that a much smarter intelligence will do what we want.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss how technological transformation could make human extinction ambiguous.
